steps.say: A scan done for something else sometimes finds a lump sitting on the adrenal gland, and that surprise has a name. An adrenal incidentaloma is an unsuspected mass that needs a triple hormone screen before anyone plans surgery. Doctors check cortisol for Cushing syndrome, metanephrines for pheochromocytoma, and the aldosterone renin ratio for Conn syndrome. Only when all three screens are negative can the lump be called truly silent.
steps.tx: Treat every **adrenal incidentaloma** (**unsuspected adrenal mass**) as guilty until proven innocent: these lesions surface on scans ordered for other reasons, so order the triple functional evaluation of overnight dexamethasone for **hypercortisolism** (cortisol excess), fractionated metanephrines for **pheochromocytoma** (adrenal medulla tumour), and aldosterone renin ratio for **aldosteronism** (aldosterone excess) before any needle or knife.

vis.alt: Adrenal adenoma gross anatomy with CT correlation and lipid rich histology.
vis.caption: Nonfunctioning adrenal adenoma: encapsulated lipid rich cortical tumour above the kidney. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Fat looks dark on a plain CT scan, and benign adrenal adenomas are full of fat. An unenhanced density under ten Hounsfield units diagnoses adenoma on the spot. Denser lesions are still proven benign when washout tops sixty percent. Denser lesions that hold onto contrast need cancer workup instead.
steps.tx: Read benignity off the scan numbers: an unenhanced attenuation under **10 Hounsfield units** (**HU**, CT density units) marks lipid rich **adrenal adenoma** (benign cortical tumour), while an **absolute washout** (contrast clearance) above **60%** (sixty percent) confirms it. Denser lesions above 20 HU with sluggish washout earn suspicion instead, so quote both numbers in every report and never call a dense slow washing mass an adenoma.

rows: Hounsfield units 10 HU or less is adenoma
Contrast washout 60 percent or more confirms benign
Above 20 HU with washout under 40 percent
Quote both numbers in every report

steps.say: Spells of pounding headache with sweating and a racing heart point at the adrenal medulla. Pheochromocytoma is a chromaffin cell tumour that dumps adrenaline into the blood in bursts. The proof is fractionated metanephrines three to four times normal in plasma or a day long urine collection. Smaller rises can come from stress or medicines, so scans wait until chemistry confirms.
steps.tx: Hunt **pheochromocytoma** (tumour of medullary **chromaffin cells**) in paroxysmal hypertension with headache, sweats, and palpitations: these **adrenal medulla** (inner gland) tumours flood blood with catecholamines. Confirm with plasma or 24 hour urinary **fractionated metanephrines** (adrenaline hormone breakdown products) raised **3 to 4 fold** (three to four times normal), since lesser rises overlap with stress and drugs, and image only after biochemistry convicts.

vis.alt: Pheochromocytoma of the adrenal medulla with catecholamine synthesis and screening rules.
vis.caption: Pheochromocytoma: chromaffin tumour, metanephrine screening, and alpha blockade before beta cover. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Operating on pheochromocytoma without preparation can kill through a pressure storm. Phenoxybenzamine blocks alpha receptors first, ten milligrams twice daily, titrated across ten to fourteen days. The endpoints are a blocked nose and a blood pressure dip on standing. Beta blockers come only after alpha cover is solid, because beta first leaves squeezing vessels unopposed.
steps.tx: Block alpha before beta, always: start **phenoxybenzamine** (irreversible alpha blocker) at **10 mg twice daily** (ten milligrams two times a day) and titrate over **10 to 14 days** (ten to fourteen days) until orthostatic hypotension and nasal stuffiness appear. Adding a **beta blocker** (heart rate drug) first leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and triggers **hypertensive crisis** (pressure explosion), so beta cover follows only established alpha blockade with volume loading.

rows: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, titrate 10 to 14 days
Orthostatic dip, stuffed nose, volume loaded
Alpha blockade first, beta cover later

steps.say: High blood pressure with stubbornly low potassium is Conn syndrome until proven otherwise. Excess aldosterone keeps sodium and dumps potassium through the kidney. Screening divides plasma aldosterone by renin, and a ratio above twenty to thirty earns confirmation. Adrenal vein sampling then tells a surgical adenoma apart from bilateral disease that needs tablets for life.
steps.tx: Pair hypertension with low potassium and think **primary hyperaldosteronism** (**Conn syndrome**, aldosterone excess): screen with the plasma **aldosterone to renin ratio** (**ARR**, hormone over enzyme) above **20 to 30** (twenty to thirty), then lateralize with **adrenal vein sampling** (**AVS**, catheter hormone assay) that separates unilateral adenoma for surgery from bilateral hyperplasia for lifelong mineralocorticoid blockade.

vis.alt: Aldosterone excess from adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia driving potassium wasting and hypertension.
vis.caption: Primary aldosteronism: adenoma versus bilateral hyperplasia, potassium wasting, and hypertension. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Most adrenal lumps are harmless, but size with density warns of cancer. Adrenocortical carcinoma usually tops four to six centimetres and looks dense and patchy with dead zones inside. Washout under forty percent is another warning sign of cancer. These masses go to full cancer surgery untouched, because a needle track can scatter tumour cells.
steps.tx: Fear big, dense, slow washing masses: **adrenocortical carcinoma** (**ACC**, adrenal cortex cancer) reaches tumour **size 4 cm** or larger, often to **6 cm** (six centimetres), shows unenhanced density above **20 HU** (twenty Hounsfield units), and washes out under **40%** (forty percent) with heterogeneous **necrosis** (dead tumour zones) and calcification. Such lesions go straight to oncologic resection without biopsy, since violated capsules seed the retroperitoneum.

vis.alt: Invasive adrenocortical carcinoma with necrosis, caval thrombus, and renal vein invasion.
vis.caption: Adrenocortical carcinoma: large necrotic invasive mass with venous thrombus. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Small benign hormone making tumours come out through keyhole cuts. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy suits functioning adenomas and single metastatic deposits under six centimetres. The surgeon takes the gland out through the belly or through the back. Big invasive cancers need open surgery with wide margins instead.
steps.tx: Prefer keyhole removal for suitable cases: **laparoscopic adrenalectomy** (keyhole gland removal) by a transperitoneal or **retroperitoneal approach** (belly or back path) is the gold standard for benign hormone making tumours and solitary **adrenal metastases** (lone spread deposits) under **6 cm** (six centimetres). Suspected carcinoma with invasion or bulk beyond this limit needs open **oncologic resection** (cancer clearance) with en bloc margins instead.

nodes.label: Benign, functioning, or solitary met under 6 cm

steps.say: A needle in the wrong adrenal lump does real harm. Biopsy can detonate a hypertensive crisis from pheochromocytoma or scatter cancer cells from adrenocortical carcinoma. Both go to surgery without sampling. Needle sampling stays reserved for one job, which is proving spread from a known cancer elsewhere when the answer changes drug treatment.
steps.tx: Keep the needle away: adrenal **biopsy** (needle sampling) is forbidden in suspected **pheochromocytoma** (catecholamine tumour) and resectable **ACC** (adrenal cancer), where puncture provokes crisis or seeds tumour. Reserve percutaneous sampling strictly for proving **metastatic disease** (spread from elsewhere) from a known extra adrenal primary when the result would change systemic therapy.
